Second Chances and First Choices

A reflection on regret, agency and the difference between being given another opportunity and choosing differently when it arrives.

3 September 20253 min read
ChoicesSecond ChancesGrowth

I learned the answer years ago, when dishonesty cost me something far greater than a job, it cost me peace of mind.

The Question That Started It

Just last week, a friend in school asked me: “What’s a complete no-no for you?” Without hesitation, I said: dishonesty.

They looked surprised. Almost as if to say, that’s a low bar.

But for me, honesty isn’t a lofty ideal. It’s the foundation. Without it, everything else collapses.

That evening, I came home and put on a movie. Its theme? Honesty. Redemption. Life giving you a second chance to do the right thing.

It felt like more than coincidence. A reminder. And it pulled me back to one of the most difficult lessons of my life.

Early Career Crossroads

After graduation in India, life was simple but intense. I was part of a close group of seven friends, all of us chasing jobs. One by one, each friend got placed. Soon, only two of us were left me and one close friend, still searching, still hopeful.

The air was filled with competition. But for us, it was also about camaraderie. We were in this together.

A Decision I Regret

And then came the interruption, the test not of my skills, but of my values.

I came across a job posting at Bosch. A big opportunity. I applied. But I didn’t tell my friend.

Why? Somewhere in me, I thought his chance meant less of mine. It was a small decision, but it shifted something inside.

Lessons in Vulnerability

When I got shortlisted, I felt a rush of excitement. I traveled to another city for the test and interview, telling myself this was my chance.

But guilt traveled with me. On the train, in the exam hall, even as I sat across from the interviewer, I kept hearing the same voice: “You should have told him.”

I flunked the interview. And oddly, I felt relief. Not because of the failure, but because deep down I knew I hadn’t earned it.

When I returned, the guilt didn’t let go. I went to my friend’s house, confessed everything, and apologized, bracing for disappointment.

The Treasure of Transparency

To my surprise, he smiled and said, “Don’t worry, I wasn’t even interested in that field.”

For him, it was nothing. For me, it was everything.

That day, I realized honesty isn’t about whether others are hurt, it’s about whether you can live with yourself.

Life didn’t give me the job. But it gave me something greater: a second chance to choose honesty.

Fast forward to now, back in school again: I no longer see classmates as competition. I see them as fellow travelers, each carrying something I can learn from. And if I don’t succeed, it isn’t because someone else got ahead, it simply means I still have more growing to do.

That experience taught me something simple: keeping things to myself doesn’t serve me, and it doesn’t serve others. So now, when I have access to information or resources, I share them. Because the real win isn’t when one of us succeeds, it’s when all of us grow together.

The treasure I carry is simple: second chances only exist to remind us to make better first choices.

Over to You

👉 What’s the one value you’d never compromise on, even if it cost you an opportunity?
